entries.title: Nigeria's jet fuel conundrum: Scarcity at home, abundance abroad
entries.summary: Nigeria is fast becoming Europe's biggest jet fuel supplier, as it continues to help ease ongoing shortages abroad. Meanwhile at home, the West African country’s own airlines are struggling to keep their tanks full.
entries.content:
August 25, 2026

Nigeria is fast becoming Europe's biggest jet fuel supplier, as it continues to help ease ongoing shortages abroad. Meanwhile at home, the West African country’s own airlines are struggling to keep their tanks full.

For the past two months. Nigeria has emerged as Europe's largest supplier of jet fuel, overtaking the United States.

The 650,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) mega refinery owned by Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote, outside Lagos has evolved into an increasingly important source of fuel for the continent following supply disruptions caused by the Iran war.

During last year's peak summer months, the majority of these supplies still originated from the Middle East.

But since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, Europe has been relying on imports of roughly 700,000 bpd in total to meet the present demands of the aviation industry, according to the private, global trade intelligence business Kpler.

Dry fuel tanks in Europe

In fact, back in April, the head of the International Energy Agency Fatih Birol expressed concern that at the time Europe only had "maybe six weeks or so" of jet fuel supplies remaining.

Less than two months later, four airports in northern Italy — Bologna, Venice, Treviso and Milan's Linate — even introduced temporary restrictions on jet fuel use, imposing a ceiling of 2,000 liters per aircraft for short-haul journeys, according to local media, while giving priority to medical and long-haul flights.

Europe has, in the meantime, been able to absorb the shock of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by diversifying its resources and boosting supplies from countries like Nigeria — but at what cost?

Paradox of surplus production

Nigeria continues to produce a record amount of jet fuel through the Dangote refinery, equivalent to about 24 million liters each day, with much of this now being shipped to Europe.

But domestic airlines in the West African country meanwhile appear to struggle to keep up with their daily estimated needs because of the surge in prices and the demands of the free market.

Ikemesit Effiong, a partner at the Africa-focused SBM intelligence consultancy, explained that "Nigeria operates a fully deregulated downstream market where Dangote prices its products with reference to international parity, not preferential domestic rates."

"Fuel flows to wherever pays the most," he told DW, adding that "currently, that is Europe, not Lagos."

"The key lesson Nigerian players are learning is that production capacity alone does not guarantee affordability at home."

While the Dangote refinery has significantly improved fuel availability in the country, which has long been plagued by chronic fuel scarcity and long queues at petrol stations, domestic prices are still among the highest on the continent.

Local airlines struggle to keep up

In the fully deregulated Nigerian market, regional airlines also have to compete with international buyers, who typically place orders for greater purchasing volumes, often without any middlemen involved between them at the refineries; according to Effiong, this alone leave global players with significant negotiating advantages compared to smaller local companies.

"The result is that [while] domestic airlines might be physically closer to the refinery, they're economically less competitive in accessing its products. They might as well be halfway across the world," he added.

Since the beginning of the crisis, local aviation operators have reportedly accrued over 60bn Naira ($45 million; €38 million) in debt to local banks to be able to sustain operations and keep afloat during this surge in prices.

Many operators have even been forced to cut key routes and hike up ticket prices, resulting in frustration and discontent among passengers; furthermore, ongoing flight cancellations and delays only keep adding to the overall sense of dissatisfaction among travelers.

At one point, jet fuel prices jumped up over threefold soon after the start of the Iran war; they have since fallen to a minimum about 1,600 Naira per liter — which compares to roughly 900 Naira prior to the war.

Hidden costs and mark-ups

The current situation is further exacerbated by the abolition of government subsidies for oil products, as well as by Nigeria's state oil company's crude-backed loans.

This means that part of the country's future crude production to is allocated to repaying debts, leaving the Dangote Refinery to have to import its crude to refine — rather than making use of Nigeria's own reserves.

But the problem isn't solely focused on the source of the jet fuel itself. Charles Victor, an energy analyst based in Lagos, explained that "[t]he journey from the refinery gate to the airport is expensive with extra layers of additional cost. [These issues include] storage, coastal shipping, moving fuel between tanks, with several traders in between — and each one takes a cut."

Victor went as far as saying that "the problem was never a supply issue. It's what happens to the price on the way to the aircraft."

No solutions without government intervention?

For Victor, the solution is to reserve a certain metric ton amount of fuel for Nigerian airlines each month, and selling this directly and equitably to all stakeholders as a group.

Buying "directly from the refinery gate, if possible, will cut out most of the middlemen adding cost along the way," he told DW, saying that wholesale price could thus at least stabilize around 1,200 Naira pet liter this way.

This plan would also require improved airport storage and distribution infrastructures to "reduce logistics costs that add significantly to the final prices," Ikemesit added. "Finally, the government should institute policies that encourage sustainable commercial relationships between Dangote and domestic carriers."

But would Dangote play along with that? The Dangote Refinery, operating at its maximum capacity of 650,000 bpd, was originally built with the intention of transforming the continent's biggest oil producer into a net exporter of refined products, and thus to end its dependence on fuel imports.

However, with a global crisis situation firmly putting Dangote on the map as a worldwide supplier, that plan might remain a pipe dream.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?
entries.summary: Iranian lawmakers have again raised the possibility of leaving a decades-old international nuclear weapons treaty. Analysts say the threat to quit may offer Tehran more leverage than an actual withdrawal.
entries.content:
Asia

Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?

August 25, 2026

Iranian lawmakers have again raised the possibility of leaving a decades-old international nuclear weapons treaty. Analysts say the threat to quit may offer Tehran more leverage than an actual withdrawal.

Lawmakers in Iran have once again raised the possibility of leaving the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as tensions over Tehran's nuclear program and its standoff with the United States continue.

Iranian MP Ghasem Ravanbakhsh said a proposal to withdraw from the landmark treaty had been submitted and was being considered.

Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the rubber-stamp parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, said withdrawal would be the "best response" to increased US economic pressure.

The idea is not new. Iranian officials and lawmakers have repeatedly raised it during periods of tension with Western governments. However, it remains unclear whether Tehran is actually preparing to leave the treaty or whether the threat itself is the objective.

What would leaving the nuclear treaty mean?

In 1970, Iran signed the agreement, which is the main international treaty on nuclear non-proliferation.

The NPT has 191 member states and is based on preventing the spread of nuclear weapons, promoting peaceful nuclear cooperation and pursuing nuclear disarmament.

Any member can withdraw if it believes that extraordinary events related to the treaty have put its supreme national interests at risk.

It must give three months' notice to the other members and the UN Security Council and explain its reasons. Leaving the treaty is therefore legally possible.

Behrooz Bayat, a nuclear expert and former consultant to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), told DW that the process would take time.

"A withdrawal would almost certainly be seen internationally as a signal that Iran intends either to keep open the option of developing nuclear weapons or to move toward doing so," Bayat said.

He said such a perception could sharply increase political and economic pressure and potentially raise the risk of further military action.

For that reason, Bayat believes Tehran's repeated threats are more useful as diplomatic leverage than as a policy it actually intends to pursue.

Why withdrawal may not benefit Tehran

Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst and researcher at LUISS University in Rome, told DW that the renewed debate should be seen in the context of stalled negotiations over uranium enrichment and Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran has about 440 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%, according to the IAEA.

Inspectors from the UN's nuclear watchdog were unable to verify the location of much of the material after the June 2025 US and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. 

Iran has already sharply reduced international oversight. In July 2025, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian signed legislation to suspend access for IAEA inspectors into the country until the "security" of its nuclear facilities is guaranteed.

That created what Modarres describes as a potentially more useful position for Tehran than formally withdrawing from the treaty.

"Withdrawal would remove that ambiguity without offering any clear advantage, turning a dispute over compliance into an explicit declaration of intent," the analyst told DW.

"By remaining formally within the NPT while limiting inspections, Iran can maintain uncertainty about its capabilities and intentions without openly leaving the global non-proliferation system," he added. "Withdrawing would remove much of that uncertainty."

A countdown could increase military risk

Withdrawal could also have security implications for Tehran. Under Article X of the treaty, states must give three months' notice before withdrawing. That period would give Israel, the United States and other governments time to reassess Iran's intentions.

Some analysts argue that governments already concerned about Iran's stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium could interpret withdrawal as a sign that Tehran was moving closer to a nuclear weapons capability.

Bayat said that makes actual withdrawal considerably less attractive than threatening to do so. He added that leaving the treaty could also "complicate Iran's civilian nuclear cooperation."

Membership in the treaty "provides the broader legal and political framework through which non-nuclear states gain access to peaceful nuclear technology," he said. "Russia remains involved in Iran's civilian nuclear sector, particularly at the Bushehr nuclear power plant."

"Formally withdrawing from the treaty could make future cooperation much more difficult politically and legally, even though existing agreements would need to be assessed separately," added Bayat.

Opposition inside Iran

There is no clear consensus in Iran. Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based analyst who has written extensively about Iran's nuclear program, told DW that withdrawing from the treaty has been discussed repeatedly but has never become government policy.

"The issue of leaving the NPT is not new and has been raised many times before," he said. "But right now, there are significant legal and political obstacles, and there is still no full consensus within Iran."

Ghahremanpour said the international community would closely examine any attempt to invoke Article X. He points to the ongoing legal debate over North Korea's withdrawal as an example.

North Korea announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003. Although Pyongyang is generally treated internationally as no longer being a party to the treaty, some UN documents note that its formal status remains uncertain.

The treaty itself, however, does not require UN Security Council approval for withdrawal. It requires only that states notify the council.

For Ghahremanpour, the political message is more important than the legal process.

He believes talk of leaving the NPT is mainly aimed at pressuring Washington, and particularly European governments, to make concessions.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Why Starlink won't open Vietnam's heavily censored internet
entries.summary: Starlink promises better connectivity in remote and mountainous areas. But in one of Southeast Asia's most tightly controlled online environments, more network access doesn't mean more free speech.
entries.content:
Vietnam

Why Starlink won't open Vietnam's heavily censored internet

August 25, 2026

Starlink promises better connectivity in remote and mountainous areas. But in one of Southeast Asia's most tightly controlled online environments, more network access doesn't mean more free speech.

Elon Musk's Starlink has begun selling satellite internet in Vietnam, bringing its high-speed service to one of the world's most tightly controlled online environments.

The satellite internet service operated by Musk's SpaceX began accepting orders from Vietnamese customers this month, with residential packages starting at around €37 ($43) a month.

Vietnam's government announced in March 2025 that it would allow SpaceX to launch Starlink on a controlled trial basis, waiving the usual restrictions on foreign ownership. The trial is capped at 600,000 subscribers and is due to run until the end of 2030.

The service is operated through Starlink Services Vietnam, a local SpaceX subsidiary established last September.

Vietnamese authorities subsequently licensed four ground gateway stations and up to 600,000 Starlink terminals for the initial rollout. The gateways allow satellite traffic to connect with terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure inside Vietnam.

Vietnam authorized the trial in March 2025 as it sought to head off threatened US trade measures over its large bilateral trade surplus.

At the time, some analysts viewed approval of Starlink, alongside tariff reductions on several US products, as part of Hanoi's effort to ease trade tensions with Washington.

Starlink comes at a high cost

Vietnam officially connected to the global internet in 1997. By the end of 2025, it had around 85.6 million internet users, equivalent to 84.2% of the population, according to government data.

Conventional internet infrastructure is already extensive. Around 85% of Vietnamese households had fiber-optic internet, while there were more than 110 million mobile broadband subscriptions, and the country's 5G network covered around 92% of the population, according to official statistics.

Starlink is relatively expensive compared to other network options, but its most obvious advantage is not in well-connected cities such as Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City but in mountainous, remote and island communities where terrestrial infrastructure remains weaker.

The Vietnamese government says Starlink could help increase internet access in remote areas, islands and places without adequate terrestrial telecommunications infrastructure.

Because satellite connections rely less on local cables and towers, they could also provide backup communications when terrestrial networks are damaged by typhoons, floods or landslides.

However, Starlink currently advertises its cheapest household plan in Vietnam at about €37 a month, while the necessary hardware starts at roughly €284.

In rural areas, where Starlink could potentially be most useful, average monthly income is just €259, according to Vietnam's National Statistics Office.

"Without subsidies, it will be unaffordable for many rural households. Its greatest impact may therefore come through shared connections for institutions such as schools, clinics and local government offices rather than individual subscriptions," Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW.

Connectivity without internet freedom

Whatever Starlink does for connectivity, there is little indication that its arrival will loosen Vietnam's increasingly tight control of online speech.

Freedom House's 2025 Freedom on the Net report gave Vietnam a score of just 22 out of 100 and classified the country's internet as "not free." Among the Asia-Pacific countries assessed, only China and Myanmar scored lower.

And foreign technology companies are already central to enforcing those restrictions.

Vietnamese authorities said Facebook, YouTube and TikTok complied with more than 94% of government requests to remove or block content during the first half of 2026.

Human Rights Watch and other rights groups have repeatedly criticized foreign platforms for facilitating state censorship.

In previous years, Hanoi publicly reported compliance rates of around 90% or higher for requests made to Facebook and YouTube to remove content the government considered illegal or anti-state.

The 2025 decision approving the Starlink pilot made clear from the outset that connectivity would remain subordinate to state security concerns, with the telecoms ministry stating that the "programme will adhere to national security and defence principles," according to the news website VNExpress.

Starlink must play by Vietnam's rules

Vietnam has also steadily expanded the legal tools available to police the internet. Decree 147, which took effect in December 2024, requires social media companies to verify users, hand over certain data and remove content deemed illegal by the authorities within 24 hours.

A new Cybersecurity Law took effect in July, further consolidating state control over cyberspace. New implementing regulations issued on August 19 allow authorities to demand that online content be removed within 24 hours and provide for accounts to be restricted or blocked for repeated violations.

The law also for the first time explicitly refers to constructing a "national firewall" to counter cybersecurity threats.

"As Vietnam is an interesting market for Starlink and the service is on a trial period, the company will ensure that it sticks to the governmental regulations rather than offering the Vietnamese citizens technical options to circumvent censorship," Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Southeast Asia at the University of Vienna, told DW.

Starlink must operate through a Vietnamese company and licensed domestic gateway stations, meaning that its service is not being introduced as a parallel internet infrastructure beyond the reach of Vietnamese regulators.

An analysis by the Singapore Space Agency last month noted that Starlink in Vietnam, unlike in most other Southeast Asian countries, will be channeled through four domestic gateway earth stations and supervised jointly by the Ministry of Science and Technology, the Ministry of National Defence and the Ministry of Public Security.

"Vietnamese instinct is risk containment through enclosure," the report noted.

According to Gerstl, "Starlink will not open a breach in the Bamboo Firewall," a reference to the nickname for Vietnam's system of legal restrictions, content controls and technical measures to regulate the internet.

"The regime will continue to uphold digital sovereignty. Indeed, censorship, currently less strict than in China, is expected to be further expanded in the future," he added.

Starlink may provide Vietnamese users with another way to get online, but it does not provide them with an internet beyond the reach of the Vietnamese state.

At best, said Giang, Starlink may broaden access to information for communities that previously had poor connectivity, which is beneficial in itself, "but better connectivity does not necessarily mean greater freedom of speech," he added.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Will tougher US sanctions disrupt Iran's shadow economy?
entries.summary: The US is expanding sanctions on Iran's financial networks, targeting crypto, gold, aviation and shipping. Analysts say the measures may fuel inflation and strengthen informal markets without changing Tehran's behavior.
entries.content:
August 25, 2026

The US is expanding sanctions on Iran's financial networks, targeting crypto, gold, aviation and shipping. Analysts say the measures may fuel inflation and strengthen informal markets without changing Tehran's behavior.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has unveiled a new phase of Washington's economic campaign against Iran, this time aimed not only at sanctioned Iranian institutions but at the international networks Tehran has used to keep money and goods moving.

Speaking on August 24, Bessent said the United States would target what he called five economic lifelines: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. He also warned foreign entities that help the country illicitly move money around.

"Any entity that facilitates money laundering for Iran will be removed from the US dollar-based financial system," Bessent said. "The countdown starts now."

The approach represents an effort to tighten secondary sanctions, putting pressure on companies, financial intermediaries and trading partners outside Iran rather than simply adding restrictions on an economy already heavily sanctioned.

The US announced measures against around 60 individuals, entities and vessels. But it stopped short of targeting major Chinese banks, highlighting the limits of how far the US may be willing to push enforcement against Iran's biggest remaining trading partner.

Closing Iran's sanctions-evasion routes

For years, Iran has relied on networks outside the formal banking system to move money.

Exchange houses, gold, cryptocurrency, front companies and opaque shipping networks have helped Iran bypass sanctions.

The latest US strategy appears designed to make those methods more difficult by increasing the cost for foreign intermediaries and comes at a vulnerable moment for Iran.

Oil exports have fallen sharply amid US efforts to disrupt Iranian oil shipments. Shipments to China, Iran's main oil customer, dropped to about 534,000 barrels per day in August from 823,000 in July and from a peak of around 1.58 million barrels earlier this year.

At home, food prices rose around 128% year on year in July, according to official data cited by Reuters news agency.

Iran's currency has lost so much value that many transactions, including property and car sales, are now conducted in US dollars. Advertisements are sometimes even priced in dollars.

Rising inflation hits Iranian businesses

The pressure is increasingly visible in ordinary businesses.

A building materials seller in the capital, Tehran, told DW that inflation has become so severe that simply holding goods can sometimes be more profitable than selling them.

"If I keep something in my warehouse for a month, its price may rise by more than the profit I would make by selling it today," he said.

He also owns a stone-cutting business and said fulfilling older contracts has become increasingly painful because replacement materials may cost considerably more a few weeks later. And raising prices offers no easy solution.

"If I increase the price beyond a certain point, nobody can afford to buy it," he said.

The restrictions also disrupt how private companies pay suppliers, import raw materials and maintain employment.

Another Iranian who works at a trading company told DW that more than 70% of its employees had been laid off during the past six months.

The company imported raw materials for various personal products and previously transferred payments through exchange houses in the United Arab Emirates.

"Now no exchange house is willing to work with us," the employee said.

Iranian businesses abroad feel the pressure

The effects are also spreading to Iranian businesspeople outside the country.

An Iranian businessman who moved to Dubai told DW that he had previously owned several cosmetics and hygiene brands in Iran. Restrictions on imports and difficulties obtaining raw materials eventually pushed him to relocate.

In Dubai things were more manageable. But since the war, that has changed, he said.

"These days, having an Iranian passport makes almost every transaction more difficult," he told DW.

He said Iranian entrepreneurs are increasingly uncertain whether banks will maintain their accounts or whether residency rules could be tightened.

"In an environment where there is no stability and the outlook is unclear, you cannot really run a business," he said.

Can more sanctions change Tehran's behavior?

Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, is skeptical that the new US measures will produce a fundamental strategic shift.

Iran is already sanctioned across most major sectors, he told DW. Further restrictions may involve expanding enforcement of existing networks rather than creating entirely new forms of economic pressure.

"Their principal effects are likely to be psychological, intensifying inflationary expectations," Salavati said.

Salavati also warns that economic pressure could weaken the remaining middle-income and professional groups that traditionally provide space for more moderate politics.

Rather than producing rapid political change, he believes the pressure could deepen polarization and encourage the state to reduce already limited subsidies and social assistance.

Will the underground economy grow?

There is another paradox. The more Washington restricts formal financial channels, the stronger the incentive becomes to develop informal ones.

Iran's sanctions economy has already created complex networks of intermediaries, cryptocurrency transfers, front companies, cash transactions and unofficial currency markets.

Closing one route may make transactions more expensive without necessarily stopping them.

"The broader consequence is likely to be corrosive rather than transformative," Salavati said, warning that the result could be an even larger and less controlled underground economy.

The new sanctions may make it harder for Tehran to finance trade, obtain foreign currency and sustain its existing economic networks. But the immediate burden is falling on companies, workers and households already dealing with wartime disruption and extreme inflation.

Whether US pressure changes the behavior of Iran's leadership remains uncertain.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: Middle East: Iran vows response to fresh US sanctions
entries.summary: Iran vowed to push back against new US "economic D-day," sanctions saying key trading partners would resist US pressure. Meanwhile, Pakistan reports progress in US-Iran mediation efforts. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Middle East

Middle East: Iran vows response to fresh US sanctions

Published August 25, 2026last updated August 25, 2026

Iran vowed to push back against new US "economic D-day," sanctions saying key trading partners would resist US pressure. Meanwhile, Pakistan reports progress in US-Iran mediation efforts. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here are the latest developments from the Iran war and the Middle East on Tuesday, August 25:

  • Iran says it is ready to respond to new US sanctions

  • China says its cooperation with Iran should not be disrupted

  • Pakistan reports progress in talks aimed at ending US-Israeli war with Iran

  • Ship disabled by attack in Strait of Hormuz

  • IMO records 68 maritime incidents since Iran war began

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Qatar calls US sanctions on Iran a unilateral move

Qatar calls US sanctions on Iran a unilateral move

Qatar described new US sanctions on Iran as a unilateral move.

The country's Foreign Ministry said it is focused on finding a diplomatic resolution to the conflict.

Qatar, Pakistan and Oman are working closely to facilitate negotiations and exchange draft proposals between Washington and Tehran.

Al Jazeera reported that the ministry also said the situation in the Strait of Hormuz should return to what it was before the start of the war.

The ministry also rejected Iran's attempt to drag regional countries into the war.

Skip next section US plans to send evacuated diplomats back to Middle East — report

US plans to send evacuated diplomats back to Middle East — report

The New York Times has reported that the United States is preparing to send diplomats evacuated before the start of the war with Iran back to the Middle East.

According to the report, US missions in the region could begin scaling back emergency measures and bringing Foreign Service officers back as early as this week.

Staffing levels were expected to increase at US missions in Israel, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Oman, Iraq and Kuwait.

The US State Department told the newspaper it was adjusting staffing based on its latest security assessment, "to ensure we can continue advancing US foreign policy objectives while protecting the safety and security of our personnel."

Skip next section Strait of Hormuz sees lowest daily vessel count since May

Strait of Hormuz sees lowest daily vessel count since May

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen sharply, with just two commodity tankers transiting the vital energy chokepoint on Monday, the lowest daily total since early May.

Shipping data from Kpler showed both vessels entered the Gulf, well below the recent daily average of 14 crossings. Some ships may not have been counted after switching off navigation transponders.

Before the conflict, the Strait of Hormuz carried about one-fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas flows.

Iran said it had blacklisted 45 tankers for violating passage rules and threatened action against vessels involved in ship-to-ship transfers with them.

Analysts said it remained unclear how Tehran would enforce those measures, but warned that any escalation or attack in the waterway could further disrupt traffic.

In a sign of how dangerous the crossing can be, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said Monday an oil tanker was hit by an "unknown projectile" off the coast of Oman.

The vessel was disabled but the crew was reported safe. It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the attack.

Skip next section WATCH — Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions?

WATCH — Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions?

Iran's leaders are acknowledging economic hardship just as the Trump administration prepares the toughest sanctions the US has ever levied against the country. Will Tehran be able to withstand another wave of economic pressure?

Skip next section China vows to protect interests after new US sanctions on Iran

China vows to protect interests after new US sanctions on Iran

China's cooperation with Iran complies with international law and should not be disrupted, a foreign ministry spokesperson said Tuesday.

"China has already stated many times that it firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions," China's Foreign Ministry Spokesman Lin Jian said.

"China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests," he added.

His statement comes after the United States on Monday targeted Iran's economic ties with the rest of the world.

"The new sectoral sanctions determinations issued today target five of Iran's most vital lifelines that it exploits in other countries: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

China is Iran's biggest trading partner and, according to the US, the primary buyer of Iranian oil.

Skip next section Gulf maritime casualties reached 20 dead, 35 injured — IMO

Gulf maritime casualties reached 20 dead, 35 injured — IMO

At least 20 seafarers and port workers were killed, 35 were wounded, and one remained missing in the Gulf and nearby waters, including the Strait of Hormuz, since the start of the Iran war, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) said.

The United Nations agency said 68 incidents had been confirmed, the equivalent of roughly one every two-and-a-half days.

About half the incidents involved oil tankers, while container ships and bulk carriers were also affected.

The rate of incidents eased after a mid-June agreement established a framework for peace talks, but rose again after those talks collapsed in early July.

Since then, four people were killed, 16 were injured, and one was reported missing as attacks and other incidents continued across the region.

Skip next section Iran vows retaliation over expanded US sanctions

Iran vows retaliation over expanded US sanctions

Iran vowed to retaliate against expanded US sanctions, saying it was "fully prepared" to respond to what it called an economic attack.

Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran had its, "own tools and know how to play the game."

His statement came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced fresh sanctions targeting 60 individuals, entities, and vessels linked to Iran.

Washington warned countries that continued trading with Iran could risk losing access to the dollar-based financial system.

You can read more about the US sanctions on Iran by clicking here. 

Skip next section Pakistan notes progress in mediation talks

Pakistan notes progress in mediation talks

Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said "significant progress" has been made in talks focused on the US-Israeli conflict with Iran and efforts to secure a path to peace.

"We remain hopeful that this momentum will help pave the way for further progress and lasting peace in the region," Naqvi wrote on social media.

Naqvi's statement came after he and Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir, a key mediator in the conflict, visited Iran. There, they held separate meetings with the president, the chief negotiator and the head of the country's highest national security body.

Pakistan's military said discussions in Tehran centered on preventing further escalation, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and bringing the conflict to an early end.

"The Iranian President candidly shared his government's perspective, and we had a very constructive ​exchange on the issues involved," Naqvi said in a post on social media.

The visit came after Munir spoke with US President Donald Trump. The White House and State Department did not immediately comment on the talks.

Pakistan has emerged as a key mediator, conveying messages and coordinating positions between Washington and Tehran.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Publicly, the United States is pursuing what it calls an "unprecedented" effort to squeeze Iran's economy by targeting its trading partners. Tehran, meanwhile, says it remains confident that key economic partners will resist Washington's pressure campaign.

At the same time, and largely away from the public spotlight, Pakistan says it is making progress in efforts to help steer the United States and Iran back toward a path of peace.

All of this is unfolding against a backdrop of mounting concerns in the Strait of Hormuz, where commodity vessel transits have fallen to a three-month low.

That is perhaps not surprising when you consider new data from the International Maritime Organization showing that 20 seafarers or port workers were killed, 35 were wounded and one remains missing during the six-monthwar involving Iran, the United States and Israel.

We'll connect these developments, and several other key stories, in our look at the Middle East today.

entries.title: Trees are vital for cooler cities, but they need help too
entries.summary: Record-breaking heat and drought are putting urban trees at risk. Experts explain how to protect these essential assets and build city forests that can withstand the climate challenges ahead.
entries.content:
August 25, 2026

Record-breaking heat and drought are putting urban trees at risk. Experts explain how to protect these essential assets and build city forests that can withstand the climate challenges ahead.

Walking beneath the trees this historically hot summer, sometimes felt like autumn had already arrived: dry, dead leaves crunching underfoot, and crowns tinged yellow or completely bare. 

That's a problem because large leafy trees help make our cities more livable. They block sunlight, reduce pollution, store carbon, provide habitats for biodiversity to thrive, soak up otherwise harmful stormwater runoff and even boost the mental and physical health of residents. 

"When trees go away, those things go away as well," Nina Bassuk, who runs the Urban Horticulture Institute at the US-based Cornell University, told DW.

That's why cities and scientists are racing to figure out how to save trees and choose smarter ones for the future.

Why cities need trees

As humans have burned fossil fuels to power industry and heat homes, the planet has become hotter, making the role of urban trees ever more vital.  

Why? Because they essentially act like giant air conditioners, which makes a big difference in hot cities. Inside a tree's canopy, temperatures can be up to three degrees cooler than the surrounding area. This is down to evapotranspiration, the process of trees absorbing water and releasing water vapor through their leaves.

In addition, trees cast shade, which keeps their surroundings from heating up in the first place.

"When we stand under a tree, the temperature we perceive can be 10 to 12 degrees Celsius (18 to 22 degrees Fahrenheit) lower than right next to it," said Matthias Beyer, a hydrologist at the Institute of Geoecology at TU Braunschweig.

And it's not just cooling. There have been numerous studies correlating all sorts of other positive effects of robust trees.

One showed that cities with more tree canopy had lower rates of cardiovascular disease. Another concluded that greener school surroundings were associated with better grades in high schools. And further research suggested that more greenspace exposure during pregnancy can lead to healthier outcomes for newborns.

How much water do trees need to survive drought?

Though a warmer climate makes trees more necessary, it also makes it harder for them to thrive. 

Healthy trees need a minimum of 10 to 15 liters of water a day, but mature ones with full foliage require up to four times that.

While there may be a temptation for cities to focus on planting new, less water-hungry trees, experts agree that the priority should be protecting older, struggling ones.

Research shows it would take around 400 saplings to replace the benefits of an old tree with a crown circumference of 20 meters. Once trees reach maturation, their benefits can be exponential, but this takes time and lots of maintenance.

"A lot of trees can't deliver the full function until 40, 50 years from the day they were planted," said Henrik Sjoman, a researcher at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences.

The best way to water trees

It's better to give trees a large amount of water over a short period so it can soak down deep, rather than letting it stay in the upper soil layers, where much of it evaporates.

For newly planted trees, a ring of metal or sturdy plastic is often fixed into the ground around the trunk. Where that's not available, a shallow depression around the tree can be created, allowing the water to pool. What matters is not damaging any surface roots in the process.

When the soil is extremely hardened, so-called irrigation bags or cushions can help. Water drips slowly but steadily into the soil through small holes on their underside. The water mustn't sit on the surface for long periods, since that can cause rot, which damages the tree.

But sometimes the soil has been heavily compacted to support sidewalks above, meaning water can't get through at all. Thirty years ago, Bassuk helped pioneer a method that mixes specially sized gravel in with the soil. It lets the stones bear the load of the sidewalk, while leaving more space for roots to stretch across dense urban ground.

"As long as you get the soil and the stone proportions right, you can compact it and yet trees can access that and grow for long distances," Bassuk said.

How to choose the right trees for cities

When it comes to climate adaptation, there's also the question of which trees to plant in the first place.  

Historically, Sjoman says urban tree selection was often driven by aesthetics and design, which led to the over-planting of single species that were vulnerable to threats like pests or disease. Horror stories of Dutch elm disease wiping out entire populations in the 20th century helped to transform urban forestry planning, placing the focus far more on diversity and climate adaptation. 

The 10-20-30 rule of thumb was coined in 1990 by the late Frank Santamour, who worked as a research geneticist at the US National Arboretum. It states that urban forest populations should include no more than 10% of any one species, 20% of a single genus or 30% of any family. 

In Germany, there are several tools and databases that offer planting guidance, and several cities are taking part in an official street tree test. The idea is that 45 species are tested at more than 220 locations to gather knowledge of how they thrive.

Another resource is the CITREE database, which categorizes almost 400 species of woody plants, sortable by more than 50 different features, including leaf density, fruit color, allergy potential, limb breakage and more.

The key feature cities need to select is drought tolerance — considering the immense biological strain urban trees are facing in an ever-warming world. But knowing the benefits trees offer a city means that is not the only factor.

"The demands of trees today — it's so much bigger, so much deeper than it was just a couple of decades ago," Sjoman said.



This article was adapted from German, with additional reporting.



Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Canada set to announce retaliatory tariffs on US goods after talks fail
entries.summary: Tariffs of 50% on Canadian goods came into effect after trade talks collapsed. US President Trump has warned Ottawa to "fall in line," but Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has refused to accept a "bad deal."
entries.content:
United States of America

Canada set to announce retaliatory tariffs on US goods

August 25, 2026

Tariffs of 50% on Canadian goods came into effect after trade talks collapsed. US President Trump has warned Ottawa to "fall in line," but Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has refused to accept a "bad deal."

Canada is set to announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, as relations between the neighbors nosedived following failed trade talks last week. 

Here's what you need to know:

  • Washington ‌and ​Ottawa were racing to reach an agreement beforeUS President Donald Trump's steep new US tariffs, announced in July, were due to take effect
  • Talks broke down days after the US President announced the neighbors were close to agreeing to a trade deal
  • The collapse in negotiations triggered Trump's threatened 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods the next day
  • Canada moved to announce its own retaliatory tariffs effective September 8

Why is Canada imposing new tariffs?

While the US and Canada have shared one of the world’s largest trade relationships, the recent talks signal a breakdown in relations.

"An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States" is "not something we’re going to accept," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

"We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum," Carney said, opting for an even blunter approach in French. "That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal."

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne and three other Cabinet ministers are expected to unveil Canada's response on Tuesday.

What did the US say?

Trump, on Monday, threatened he would impose a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, car parts and steel from January 1, 2027, and took to social media to unleash a tirade against the historic partner.

"On trade, ‌and in other ways, also, ‌they ​are among the worst nations in the world to deal with. They feel entitled, and ​yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!" the US president said.

Canada relies heavily on the US as its top trading partner, with American-bound exports making up 70% of the country's total. The relationship runs both ways, too: government data shows Canada was the second-largest US trading partner in goods this year, just behind Mexico.

No further negotiations are currently scheduled.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Germany news: Third drone found in Leipzig airport probe
entries.summary: German media say investigators have found a third drone and suspected explosives linked to the Leipzig/Halle Airport incident. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Third drone found in Leipzig airport probe

Published August 25, 2026last updated August 25, 2026

German media say investigators have found a third drone and suspected explosives linked to the Leipzig/Halle Airport incident. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, August 25, 2026:

  • German media say investigators found a third drone near Leipzig/Halle Airport, along with suspected explosives
  • Merz says Germany will identify the suspected attackers soon
  • Security sources reportedly suspect Russian intelligence involvement, which Moscow denies
  • German economy grows for third straight quarter
  • Crisis talks between management and workers start at VW

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Germans swap friends for screens in their free time

Germans swap friends for screens in their free time

Germans are spending less of their free time socializing with friends and more on individually planned and digital activities, according to a new representative survey.

The Hamburg Foundation for Future Studies found that just 19% of 3,000 respondents said they regularly went out with friends, down from 37% when its first "Leisure Monitor" was conducted 40 years ago.

Meeting friends remains the most important social leisure activity, but its role has weakened significantly over time.

"Traditional sociability is losing reach, while social contacts are increasingly shifting toward individually planned and digital forms," said Ulrich Reinhardt, the foundation's scientific director.

He said everyday leisure was increasingly dominated by internet use, television, music and smartphones. Digital activities have grown sharply:

  • 82% listen to music digitally at least weekly, up from 52% in 2016.
  • 71% use social media weekly, up from 48%.
  • 33% play video games weekly, up from 9%.

Artificial intelligence is now used at least once a week by 42% of respondents, rising to 62% among 18- to 24-year-olds.

Reinhardt said younger users were turning to AI not just for information, but also for advice, reassurance and, in some cases, as a substitute for friendship.

Skip next section Zelenskyy thanks Germany for support for Ukraine

Zelenskyy thanks Germany for support for Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has thanked Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Germany for their support for Ukraine's defence and independence.

"Countless lives have been saved thanks to German aid," Zelenskyy wrote on X, praising both Berlin's bilateral assistance and its role in rallying wider international support.

Zelenskyy was responding to a message from Merz marking Ukraine's Independence Day.

The German chancellor wrote simply: "Slawa Ukrajini!" — "Glory to Ukraine!"

Zelenskyy ended his reply with "Heroyam Slava!" — "Glory to the heroes!"

Germany has been one of Ukraine's biggest military and financial supporters since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Skip next section Suspected sabotage disrupts trains and communications near Stuttgart

Suspected sabotage disrupts trains and communications near Stuttgart

German police are investigating suspected sabotage after several cables were cut along a railway line near the town of Backnang, northeast of Stuttgart.

The damage disrupted train services as well as internet and telephone connections in the town of around 38,000 people.

Police said unknown perpetrators gained access to a concrete shaft beside the railway tracks between Backnang and the Maubach district on Sunday afternoon.

Several cables were then cut using tools.

It was not immediately clear how many trains were affected or how long the disruption lasted.

The state security division has taken over the investigation on suspicion of sabotage.

Police said they could not completely rule out the possibility that legitimate work had been taking place at the site, but added that rail operator Deutsche Bahn would normally have been informed of such work.

Investigators are appealing for witnesses who noticed suspicious activity on nearby paths or hiking trails.

Skip next section German construction sector posts strong June growth

German construction sector posts strong June growth

Germany's construction sector has recorded a sharp increase in orders, sales and employment, official data has shown.

New orders in the main construction industry rose 11.3% year on year in June after adjusting for prices and calendar effects, while inflation-adjusted sales increased 6.6%, according to the Federal Statistical Office.

Large orders helped boost activity in both building construction, which includes housing, as well as civil engineering projects such as roads and bridges.

Orders also rose strongly over the broader April-to-June period.

Employment increased by 1.5% from a year earlier to around 545,000 people in June.

"The month of June was a good one for the construction industry," said Felix Pakleppa of the ZDB construction association.

However, he cautioned that after a volatile first half of the year it was too early to speak of a sustained turnaround.

The industry is benefiting from billions of euros in federal spending on roads, railways and other infrastructure.

Housing construction remains weaker, partly because higher interest rates have made building more expensive for households and investors.

Skip next section Merz says Germany will soon identify Leipzig drone attackers

Merz says Germany will soon identify Leipzig drone attackers

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said the German government will "shortly" set out who it believes was behind the August 4 drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport.

"They will pay for it," Merz said Tuesday before a Cabinet retreat in the state of Brandenburg, adding that authorities were working intensively to establish responsibility.

Merz said the incident showed Germany was increasingly becoming a target for hybrid attacks.

"Attackers are increasingly prepared to accept serious property damage, and even injuries and deaths, without scruple," he said.

He said the government was strengthening its response, including through a new drone defense center in Magdeburg.

Investigators believe an explosives-laden drone was deliberately directed toward a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport on August 4.

Skip next section One in 12 long-distance trains canceled in Germany

One in 12 long-distance trains canceled in Germany

Almost one in 12 long-distance trains operated by Deutsche Bahn was canceled entirely or for part of its route in the first half of 2026, according to government figures.

The cancellation rate reached 8%, up three percentage points from the same period last year and the second-highest level since 2019.

The figures come from a Transport Ministry response to a parliamentary question from the Greens.

Only the first half of 2024 saw a higher cancellation rate, at 12%, largely because of strikes by the German Train Drivers' Union (GDL).

Deutsche Bahn said only 3.6% of affected ICE (Intercity Express) and IC (Intercity) services were canceled without replacement.

The state-owned rail operator said most passengers were able to use alternative connections, including when trains failed to reach their final destination.

It cited severe winter weather in January and extreme heat in June among the reasons for disruption.

Skip next section Volkswagen workers demand answers over sweeping cuts

Volkswagen workers demand answers over sweeping cuts

Volkswagen workers have begun a series of extraordinary staff meetings as pressure mounts on management over planned cost-cutting measures that could put thousands of jobs and four plants at risk.

The first meeting is taking place at the carmaker's headquarters in Wolfsburg, where employee representatives are demanding greater clarity from the board.

Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume has said the savings announced so far will not be enough.

"We are oversized. That often makes us too slow and too complicated," Blume said, describing the company's situation as "more than critical."

He argued that Volkswagen's problems reflected a wider crisis across the auto industry rather than a crisis at VW alone.

Blume cited US tariffs, a sharp downturn and falling prices in China, geopolitical tensions, tougher competition in Europe and extensive regulation as major challenges.

Employee representatives say the board has failed to explain clearly how it plans to make the company competitive under those conditions.

An internal survey cited in a company intranet article found strong dissatisfaction with management communication, saying workers and their families had been left "uncertain and afraid."

Skip next section Germany to choose its Oscar contender

Germany to choose its Oscar contender

Germany is set to choose which film will represent the country in the race for the 2027 Academy Awards.

A jury is meeting in Munich over two days to select one of 11 films, with the decision due to be announced Tuesday evening.

The contenders include Simon Verhoeven's literary adaptation "Oh, This Unspeakable Void" ("Ach, diese Lücke, diese entsetzliche Lücke") and veteran director Volker Schlöndorff's historical drama "Visitation" ("Heimsuchung").

More explicitly political entries include Faraz Shariat's courtroom drama "Prosecution" ("Staatsschutz"), about far-right violence, and Markus Goller's "23,000 Lives" ("23 000 Leben"), about migrant rescue operations in the Mediterranean.

Other candidates include Valeska Grisebach's "The Dreamed Adventure" ("Das geträumte Abenteuer"), Andrey Zvyagintsev's "Minotaur" ("Minotaurus") and Sandra Wollner's "Everytime."

Germany last won the international feature Oscar in 2023 with Edward Berger's anti-war drama "All Quiet on the Western Front."

The film won four Academy Awards in total.

Skip next section German Cabinet meets after reshuffle

German Cabinet meets after reshuffle

Germany's government has begun a two-day Cabinet retreat in its new line-up, with efforts to strengthen the country's economic competitiveness at the top of the agenda.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his ministers are meeting at Neuhardenberg Palace in Brandenburg, where they will also discuss the consequences of this summer's extreme heat.

The main focus is expected to be Germany's struggling competitiveness and measures to strengthen the economy.

At the retreat, ministers from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the junior partner in Merz's coalition, are expected to push for a constitutional change to strengthen climate action. The move is opposed by Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Merz reshuffled his government in July after the resignation of parliamentary group leader Jens Spahn.

Former Health Minister Nina Warken became head of the Chancellery, while former CDU Secretary-General Carsten Linnemann took over the Health Ministry.

Steffen Bilger, previously a senior parliamentary manager for the conservative CDU/CSU group, replaced Patrick Schnieder as transport minister.

The way Schnieder was removed prompted considerable criticism within the CDU, making the retreat an early test of how smoothly the newly assembled Cabinet can work together.

Neuhardenberg Palace last hosted a Cabinet retreat in 2004, when Germany was governed by the SPD-Green coalition of Chancellor Gerhard Schröder and Vice Chancellor Joschka Fischer.

Skip next section German economy records better-than-expected growth in second quarter

German economy records better-than-expected growth in second quarter

Germany's economy grew by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2026, slightly more strongly than initially estimated, official data shows.

The Federal Statistical Office, known as Destatis, revised its preliminary estimate up from 0.2%, saying exports and stronger-than-expected retail and wholesale activity helped drive the improvement.

Exports of goods and services rose by 2.0% from the previous quarter, with goods exports up 2.6%.

Imports increased by 1.5% overall. GDP was 1% higher than in the second quarter of 2025.

"The growth momentum in the German economy from the start of the year is continuing," Destatis President Ruth Brand said, adding that exports were again the main driver.

Despite the good news, investment remained subdued:

  • Equipment investment fell 1.4%
  • Overall fixed investment declined 0.2%
  • Construction investment edged up just 0.1%
  • Private and government consumption each increased 0.1%

Europe's largest economy has now grown for three consecutive quarters.

Skip next section Third drone found after Leipzig airport attack — reports

Third drone found after Leipzig airport attack — reports

German investigators have discovered a third drone and suspected explosives linked to an incident at Leipzig/Halle airport earlier this month, according to German media.

The drone was found on August 14, 10 days after the incident, west of the airport. Investigators reportedly discovered around 50 grams (1.8 ounces) of a substance suspected to be the military explosive hexogen.

The initial reports came from public broadcasters NDR and WDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper.

On August 4, an explosives-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies.

Investigators also suspect a second drone may have collided with a DHL cargo aircraft shortly after the airport was temporarily closed.

Security sources cited by the German media reports suspect Russian intelligence involvement.

Russia has denied accusations that it was behind the attempted attack.

Leipzig/Halle is one of Germany's most important cargo airports and also serves as a military logistics hub.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

You join us as investigators are reported to have found a third drone and suspected explosives linked to a security incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport earlier this month.

German media said the drone was discovered on August 14, around 10 days after the original incident, west of the airport.

Security sources cited by German media suspect Russian intelligence involvement.

We'll also be following the first government retreat since the summer break, the latest economic forecasts for Germany and the crisis talks at struggling car giant Volkswagen.

And Germany will be deciding which films it submits for an Oscar nomination.

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

entries.title: Australia's music chart bars fully AI-generated music
entries.summary: The ARIA chart is drawing a line between artists who use AI as a tool and songs created largely by machines.
entries.content:
Australia

Australia's music chart bars fully AI-generated music

August 25, 2026

The ARIA chart is drawing a line between artists who use AI as a tool and songs created largely by machines.

Australia's official music charts will no longer allow wholly AI-generated tracks to qualify, under new rules announced by the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA).

The changes take effect with the ARIA chart dated August 31 and distinguish between music generated primarily by artificial intelligence and recordings where AI is used only as a supporting creative tool.

What AI music will still be allowed in Australia's charts?

Recordings made with generative AI can remain eligible if they are substantially human-made and do not raise concerns about manipulation of streams or chart positions.

ARIA will use an industry-wide distinction announced in July between:

  • AI-generated music, where AI creates all or the main creative elements of a recording
  • AI-assisted music, which remains substantially human-created but uses generative AI for some elements

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said artists were already using AI creatively and the charts should allow room for that.

"This gives everyone who releases music in Australia a clear rule to work to. We call on all parties who have a role in deciding the music played and promoted to Australian audiences, particularly radio, to support human artistry and implement similar changes across their own codes," said Herd.

What happens if an AI track enters the charts?

ARIA can refuse to accept an ineligible recording, remove it from the charts either retrospectively or in advance, change chart positions and withdraw accreditations.

It can also revoke an ARIA No. 1 Award, while an ineligible track will not qualify for an ARIA Award. Artists and their representatives will be able to challenge exclusions and provide evidence that a recording meets the rules.

The move is part of a broader initiative led by the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), which represents the recording industry globally.

IFPI announced principles in July intended for use across official charts internationally. They require eligible AI-assisted recordings to remain substantially human-made, use lawful and authorized AI services and avoid artificial manipulation of streams.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: US: Trump administration plans to revoke up to 200,000 visas from asylum seekers
entries.summary: The State Department is reportedly looking to revoke the visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who sought asylum after entering on tourist or business visas, in what could be the largest mass visa revocation in US history.
entries.content:
United States of America

US plans mass visa revocation for asylum seekers

August 25, 2026

The State Department is reportedly looking to revoke the visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who sought asylum after entering on tourist or business visas, in what could be the largest mass visa revocation in US history.

United States President Donald Trump's administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of foreigners who applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the country, the State Department said in a statement on Monday. 

It didn't say how many visas would be affected, but the Associated Press put the number at up to 200,000, citing State Department documents ‌and ​two US officials. If carried out, it would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history.

What did the State Department say about revoking visas?

The State Department is expected to announce the revocations in the coming weeks, targeting so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to holders who have sought or are now seeking asylum. These visas are generally issued for business travel, tourism, family visits or medical care. 

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said, referring to the Department of Homeland Security.

He declined to give a specific number, saying the count "remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

Officials said the revocations would not necessarily lead to immediate deportation. Most people with pending asylum cases would instead be recategorized, losing their status as business or tourism travelers, according to officials who spoke to AP on condition of anonymity.

Trump official slams visa use

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau criticized the use of tourist and business visas as a path to asylum claims.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," he wrote on social media platform X, adding, "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

He separately alleged that the US immigration system "has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims" and cited the case of a Colombian national who entered the US on a tourist visa in 2015 before applying for asylum.

Applicants for B1 and B2 visas are currently required to affirm they will not seek asylum and to demonstrate intent to return to their home countries. It remains unclear how many current visa holders have actually filed for asylum.

Who has been impacted by Trump's immigration crackdown?

The move is the latest in a series of visa restrictions under Trump's second term, which has included expanded social media vetting, new bond requirements, and outright bans on visa issuance for citizens of certain countries. 

The State Department said it has revoked roughly 175,000 visas over the past 18 months, citing reasons ranging from criminal convictions to public criticism of US policy, particularly regarding the Middle East. The administration has also targeted "birth tourism," and has repeatedly sought to end birthright citizenship. Courts, including the Supreme Court, have rejected those efforts.

Rights groups have criticized the broader immigration crackdown, arguing it has infringed on free speech and due process rights while creating an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities who could face racial profiling. The administration maintains the crackdown is intended to strengthen domestic security. 

Despite campaigning largely on illegal immigration, the administration has also tightened legal immigration pathways, including through new, costly fees for certain work visa applicants. Several aspects of the crackdown are facing ongoing legal challenges.

Edited by: Rob Turner
